rationale: Both speak of faith apart from ordinary sight. Corinthians describes walking through faith rather than sight; Hebrews describes assurance of hoped-for things and conviction concerning unseen realities. Their precise definitions and surrounding situations remain distinct.

The following Abel account is an explicit example of testimony through faith: he receives testimony of righteousness. This provides a concrete instance of the elders testimony rather than reducing every elder to Abel or supplying all later examples in one verse.

Genesis narrates God making heaven and earth and speaking light into being. Hebrews names the ages formed by Gods word and adds an inference about visible things. Genesis does not itself print that entire unseen-origin formulation.

Genesis narrates Cain and Abel bringing gifts and the Lords differing regard for them. Hebrews gives its faith-and-righteousness interpretation and the dead-still-speaking statement. Those explanatory clauses are not silently inserted into the Genesis narrative.

The Enoch account corresponds to pleasing God and no longer being found because God took him. The actual supplied removal wording and Hebrews added faith/no-death interpretation remain as printed rather than substituting a familiar other-edition formulation.

relationship: pleasing God through faith in context
rationale: The preceding Enoch account explicitly connects faith and testimony that he pleased God. It provides the immediate case beside this faith requirement. This verse additionally names believing God is and rewards seekers, which are not all repeated in the Enoch unit.

Genesis gives the announced flood, ark entry for Noahs household and his compliance with Gods commands. Hebrews describes faith, unseen warning and the resulting righteousness account. The latter interpretive predicates are not substituted for the narrative instructions.

relationship: call to leave for a shown land
rationale: Genesis commands Abram to leave for the land God will show and narrates his departure. Hebrews names Abraham and describes obedience through faith without knowing the destination. The printed Abram/Abraham forms and the additional promises remain distinct.

Genesis names Jacob coming to Isaac at the place where Abraham and Isaac sojourned. This provides a concrete place-and-patriarch counterpart to the sojourning description. The unit is not made to say all three lived in tents together at one time.

The later explanation says God prepared a city for those desiring a heavenly homeland. This gives an explicit divine-city counterpart to awaiting the city whose maker is God. Neither unit is completed with an unprinted city name.

Genesis narrates the Lord doing for Sarah as He spoke and her bearing the promised son. This provides the narrative promise counterpart to her considering the Promiser faithful. Hebrews adds its faith, barrenness and beyond-age descriptions.

The promise that offspring will multiply like heavens stars and seashore sand corresponds to the two images here. Genesis gives the promise; Hebrews describes the multitude born from one as good as dead. The promise and fulfillment descriptions remain distinct.

Abrahams self-description among the people during a burial request provides a concrete confession beside Hebrews strangers-and-sojourners wording. The Genesis speaker is alive in that scene; the source account of dying in faith is not inserted into the burial-request unit.

The preceding confession of being strangers and sojourners supplies the stated words behind those who say such things. Hebrews then infers seeking a homeland. The inference is distinguished from the quoted confession itself.

relationship: return to the departure country discussed
rationale: Genesis discusses taking Abrahams son back to the country of departure and records Abrahams refusal. This is a specific return-country comparison for Hebrews counterfactual opportunity statement, without claiming every patriarch made that exact narrated decision.

relationship: God called God of the patriarchs
rationale: Gods self-identification as God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob supplies a concrete counterpart to being called their God. Hebrews adds not being ashamed, a better heavenly homeland and a prepared city; those clauses are not inserted into Exodus.

Genesis narrates the test, commanded offering, binding and halted killing of Isaac. Hebrews describes offering by faith and the welcomed promises. The actual son descriptors and the distinction between offering and completed killing remain in each passage.

The in-Isaac offspring declaration directly corresponds to Genesis21:12. The Genesis unit also addresses Sarahs words and the other child context; Hebrews quotes the declaration within the Isaac-offering account without reproducing every surrounding clause.

relationship: Abraham faith and God giving life to dead
rationale: Both associate Abraham-related faith with Gods power over death. Romans names God giving life to the dead; Hebrews reasons that He can raise the dead and calls Isaacs reception figurative. No literal completed death of Isaac is asserted.

This part of Genesis gives the blessing spoken to Jacob, one of the two sons named here. Hebrews additionally names Esau and faith concerning things to come. This pair covers Jacobs portion rather than claiming the target also narrates Esaus blessing.

This separate part of Genesis gives Isaacs words to Esau. Together with the separately retained Jacob passage it supplies both named blessings, while the distinct words and circumstances remain intact. The second pair adds no second source completion.
